vanishes only in the limit $\theta\to1$.  Up to the usual tie break at
the top

$x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)$,

i.e. the best reply is the lenient auditor on the whole interior of the
type space.  In the weak set order the best reply is constant $x^{*}\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$ and it is (weakly) monotone towards leniency as $\theta$
rises: a firm that raises its truthfulness from $\theta'$ to
$\theta''<1$ stays with $x=0$, so the comparative static that is normally
quoted as “more truthful $\Rightarrow$ (weakly) more lenient’’ is realised
on the entire interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the knife-edge indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  On the conventional
discrete support this is the statement that the lenient auditor is the
unique best response for every $\theta<1$, essentially the set
$\theta\in[0,1)$.  The indifference at $\theta=1$ is the only boundary
case; apart from it the monotone sorting towards leniency is the
familiar interior result.

5.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the relevant part of the expected outlay is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{ {\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
        =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta) ,
\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\ell (\theta ,x) ,
$$

so that on the two point support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) .
$$

Put $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$.  $F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$
imply

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta )F'(\theta)<0 ,
\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$ and $h(\theta)>0$ for
$\theta<1$.  Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)
      =p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

$$
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\Big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\Big]<0,
$$

i.e. the extra expected penalty of the strict auditor is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

so that the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique best reply for every
non-perfect type and the perfectly truthful type is indifferent. In the
conventional tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}(\cdot)$ is constant on the interior of the type space and
weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$.  With $A(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]\,
     \big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

whenever $xp(x)$ is increasing at $x$, so that $C(\theta,x)-C(\theta,x')$
is decreasing in $\theta$ for $x>x'$.  The strict auditor becomes
relatively cheaper as $\theta$ rises, $h(\theta)\downarrow$, and the
cost disadvantage $\Delta(\theta)$ of $x=1$ falls with truthfulness.
Hence in the strict preference sense there is no interior type at which
an increase in $\theta$ induces a strict move to a smaller $x$:
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and the strict monotone decreasing
comparative static is vacuous, the empty set.  Modulo the knife edge
indifference $\theta=1$ this is the weak statement $x^{*}=0$ for every
$0\le\theta<1$, i.e. the lenient auditor is the unique, $x$-independent,
best response for the whole interior of the type space and the
malpractice type is the one which strictly wants leniency.  The
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ is the only boundary case. ∎

3.text:
For the $x$--dependent part of the expected outlay write

$$
\ell(\theta ,x):=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x),
$$

so that up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}=k'(\theta)h'(x) .
$$

$1-\theta$ is strictly decreasing and $F$ is decreasing, hence

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
k(\theta)>0\;{\rm for}\;\theta<1,\;k(1)=0,
$$

and $k(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.  On the two point
support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
          =p(1)k(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  In
particular

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-perfect type and the
two auditors are indifferent for the perfectly truthful type.  Hence
with the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le \theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the disadvantage of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\bigl[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,\qquad 
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In the Spence–Mirrlees sense

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\Big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\Big]\,
   \Big[p(x)+xp'(x)\Big]<0
$$

whenever $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, so that $\partial C/\partial x$ is
decreasing in $\theta$.  The cost of moving $0\to1$ falls with
$\theta$ and the optimal strictness is weakly non-decreasing in
$\theta$.  In the binary $0/1$ formulation the best reply is the
constant $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$ and is
indifferent only at the knife edge $\theta=1$.  In the strict preference
sense there is therefore no interior $\theta$ at which a rise in
truthfulness strictly induces a strict move to a more lenient auditor;
the strictly monotone decreasing comparative static is vacuous, the
only boundary being the indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  Up to the
conventional tie break this is the trivial weak statement
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for every non-perfect type $\theta\in[0,1)$, with
$x^{*}=0$ the unique best reply for all $\theta<1$ and indifference at
$\theta=1$.  This is the reversal of the usual signalling intuition:
the more truthful type can afford the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ and the
reputation benefit $p(x)\downarrow$, so optimal $x^{*}$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$, not decreasing. ∎

public_text.2:
With the $x$–independent tax $t(\theta)$ dropped the relevant expected
outlay is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\ell (\theta ,x) ,
$$

and on the binary support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta ),
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta (\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)h(\theta), \qquad h(\theta)=(1-\theta )F(\theta)>0 .
$$

$F$ decreasing and $1-\theta$ decreasing imply

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0 ,\qquad 
h(1)=0 ,
$$

hence $h(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and $h$ is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1]$.  In particular

$$
\Delta (\theta)>0 \iff \theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0, 
\qquad\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0
$$

on the interior.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, i.e. with the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$, the truthful limit being indifferent.  The
extra expected penalty of the strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$, $\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.  Hence the cost disadvantage of $x=1$ relative to
$x=0$ falls with truthfulness.  In the strict preference sense
$x^{*}(\cdot)$ is constant on $[0,1)$,

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]>0
$$

for the empirically relevant $xp(x)$ decreasing case, so that
$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and the best reply is
weakly increasing in $\theta$.

In particular there is no interior $\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ in the strict sense; the strict
monotone decreasing comparative static is vacuous.  Up to the trivial
indifference at the top the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique best
response for every non-perfect type, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, and the
only boundary case is $\Delta(1)=0$.  This is the weak statement
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ on the interior and the strict statement that the
set of $\theta$ on which a strict increase in truthfulness induces a
strict move to a more lenient auditor is empty, the conventional
sorting being $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$, i.e.
more truthful firms can be made to bear the strict auditor.  With the
usual weak dominance convention the lenient auditor dominates on the
whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, with indifference only at $\theta=1$. ∎
public_text.8:

                =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,

h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 .

$$

i.e. the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor

$$

cheaper.  In the strict preference sense there is no interior type at

whole interior $0\le\theta<1$ and the only non-trivial boundary is the
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.

best response on the essentially relevant interior $0<\theta<1$ and the
truthful type $\theta=1$ is the degenerate indifference point.  Strictly
speaking the monotone decreasing comparative static $x^{*}(\theta)\downarrow$
is vacuous on the interior, the strict set being empty. ∎
public_text.1:
Up to the $x$–free tax $t(\theta)$ the relevant part of the expected
payment is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )=k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 ,
$$

so that 
$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=:\Delta(\theta).
$$

$F$ decreasing and $1-\theta$ decreasing gives
$k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$k(1)=0$, hence with $p(1)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and
$$
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 .
$$

Hence on the binary support
$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad \theta<1,
$$
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. up to the knife edge $\theta=1$ the best reply is the constant
$x^{*}\equiv0$.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[-F+(1-\theta)F'\big]\big[p+xp'\big]<0
$$

for $p+xp'>0$, so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and
the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor $\Delta(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  A higher $\theta$ makes the strict
auditor relatively cheaper, $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in
$\theta$, and in the strict preference sense there is no interior
$\theta$ at which an increase of truthfulness induces a strict move to a
more lenient, i.e. a strictly smaller, auditor. The strictly monotone
decreasing set is empty.

Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique best response on the whole
interior, $x^{*}=0$ for every $\theta<1$, the advantage of leniency
being $\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$.  The only boundary
case is the indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful type,
so that with the conventional weak formulation the lenient auditor is
(weakly) optimal for $\theta\in[0,1)$ and the strict preference for
leniency disappears at $\theta=1$.  This is the familiar perverse
constant choice $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$. ∎
public_text.4:
With the $x$ free part of the expected outlay

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+{\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}\,p(x)F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
      =t(\theta )+k(\theta )h(x) ,
$$

$$
k(\theta )=(1-\theta )F(\theta )>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 ,
$$

$t(\theta )$ being $x$–free.  On the two point support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta )+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta ) ,
$$

i.e. up to the common $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta (\theta ): =C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta )
               =p(1)k(\theta )\ge 0,
$$

with $k(1)=0$ and $k$ strictly decreasing because $1-\theta$ and $F$
are decreasing,

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0 ,\qquad 
k(\theta_{2})<k(\theta_{1})\iff\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;,
$$

so that

$$
 \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
\qquad \Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 .
$$

Hence for every non-perfect type the expected penalty of the strict
auditor is strictly positive and the strict auditor is strictly
dominated by the lenient one,

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad 0\le \theta<1,
$$

and

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

the perfectly truthful type being indifferent.  The disadvantage of
strictness

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$, i.e. the incremental cost of moving
from $x=0$ to $x=1$ falls with truthfulness.  In the usual
Spence–Mirrlees form

$$
C(\theta_{2},x_{2})-C(\theta_{2},x_{1})-
C(\theta_{1},x_{2})+C(\theta_{1},x_{1})
   =\bigl[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})\bigr]\,
    \bigl[h(x_{2})-h(x_{1})\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta_{2}>\theta_{1},~x_{2}>x_{1},
$$

and
$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big],
$$
so that $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ whenever
$h(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing.  Hence with the conventional $h'>0$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$, i.e. the best reply is (weakly) increasing
in $\theta$.  The lenient auditor is the unique strict best reply on the
whole interior $0\le\theta<1$ and it is the stationary best reply.
In strictly monotone terms there is therefore no interior $\theta_{2}>
\theta_{1}$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the strictly
decreasing comparative static $ \theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$
is vacuous on the interior and the strict preference for a more lenient
auditor generated by a rise in truthfulness is the empty set.  Up to the
usual tie-break the lenient auditor is weakly optimal for every
$\theta\in[0,1)$, with the only non-trivial boundary being the
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful limit $\theta=1$.
With the conventional weak ordering this is normally phrased as
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, i.e. the lenient auditor is the unique best
response for all non-perfect types and the truthful limit is
indifferent.  This is the familiar reversal of the signalling intuition:
a higher $\theta$ makes a strict auditor relatively cheaper, so that in
the weak set order optimal strictness is non-decreasing in truthfulness. ∎

The relevant part of expected payment that depends on x is

$C_1(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ up to the additively separable tax $t(\theta)$.
On the binary support

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so that, up to $t(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$,
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$.

$F$ is decreasing and $1-\theta$ is decreasing, hence $h$ and therefore
$\Delta$ are strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$ with $h(1)=0$. In particular

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$,

and

$\Delta(\theta_2)<\Delta(\theta_1)$ for every $\theta_2>\theta_1$.

Hence the expected cost disadvantage of the strict auditor relative to the
lenient auditor is strictly positive for every non-truthful type and it
falls strictly with truthfulness.  Up to the knife-edge indifference at
$\theta=1$ the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique best reply:

$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$.

In words the (strict) penalty saving from staying with the lenient
auditor is $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ and this saving is monotone
decreasing in $\theta$.  A marginal increase in truthfulness therefore
reduces the extra expected penalty that would be incurred by a refusal
under a strict auditor, i.e. the firm’s willingness to stay with the
lenient technology persists and is in fact the economically relevant
choice on the whole interior.  The conventional interior statement is
that on $0<\theta<1$ the best reply is constantly the lenient one,
$x^{*}\equiv0$, so that more truthful types continue to choose the
lenient auditor and the lenient auditor is weakly preferred for the
entire interior set $\theta<1$, with the usual limit indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful type.  In the usual weak
formulation this is the set $[0,1)$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, on which
higher truthfulness is associated with the lenient choice $x=0$ and the
cost advantage of leniency is monotone decreasing in $\theta$. ∎

i.e. optimal strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness.  In
strict monotone terms there is therefore no interior $\theta$ at which
an increase in truthfulness induces a strict move to a strictly more
lenient auditor.  The strict comparative static $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
constant $0$ on $[0,1)$ and indeterminate at $1$; the strictly
decreasing sorting $x^{*}\!\downarrow\!\theta$ is vacuous, the empty
set.

Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ dominates the strict auditor $x=1$
for the whole interior, $C(\theta ,0)\le C(\theta ,1)$ with strict
inequality for $0\le\theta<1$, and the only knife–edge case is the
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  This is usually phrased as the weak
dominance $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the
familiar "more truthful $\Rightarrow$ weakly more willing to use the
strict auditor" sorting. ∎

The relevant part of the expected payment is the penalty exposure

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$

up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$.  With the two admissible types

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so that on the penalty part

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
=p(1)h(\theta)$,
$h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$.

$F$ decreasing gives $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$
and $h(1)=0$.  Hence

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$,

and $\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1]$.

In particular the lenient auditor $x=0$ is strictly dominant for every
non-truthful type.  The extra expected cost of the strict auditor is
positive for $\theta<1$ and shrinks with truthfulness, so the gain from
staying with the lenient auditor is maximal for low $\theta$ and
vanishes only in the limit $\theta\to1$.  Up to the usual tie break at
the top

$x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)$,

i.e. the best reply is the lenient auditor on the whole interior of the
type space.  In the weak set order the best reply is constant $x^{*}\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$ and it is (weakly) monotone towards leniency as $\theta$
rises: a firm that raises its truthfulness from $\theta'$ to
$\theta''<1$ stays with $x=0$, so the comparative static that is normally
quoted as “more truthful $\Rightarrow$ (weakly) more lenient’’ is realised
on the entire interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the knife-edge indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  On the conventional
discrete support this is the statement that the lenient auditor is the
unique best response for every $\theta<1$, essentially the set
$\theta\in[0,1)$.  The indifference at $\theta=1$ is the only boundary
case; apart from it the monotone sorting towards leniency is the
familiar interior result.

Up to the $x$ free tax the relevant part of the expected outlay is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{ {\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
        =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta) ,
\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\ell (\theta ,x) ,
$$

so that on the two point support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) .
$$

Put $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$.  $F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$
imply

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta )F'(\theta)<0 ,
\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$ and $h(\theta)>0$ for
$\theta<1$.  Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)
      =p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

$$
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\Big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\Big]<0,
$$

i.e. the extra expected penalty of the strict auditor is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

so that the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique best reply for every
non-perfect type and the perfectly truthful type is indifferent. In the
conventional tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}(\cdot)$ is constant on the interior of the type space and
weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$.  With $A(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]\,
     \big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

whenever $xp(x)$ is increasing at $x$, so that $C(\theta,x)-C(\theta,x')$
is decreasing in $\theta$ for $x>x'$.  The strict auditor becomes
relatively cheaper as $\theta$ rises, $h(\theta)\downarrow$, and the
cost disadvantage $\Delta(\theta)$ of $x=1$ falls with truthfulness.
Hence in the strict preference sense there is no interior type at which
an increase in $\theta$ induces a strict move to a smaller $x$:
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and the strict monotone decreasing
comparative static is vacuous, the empty set.  Modulo the knife edge
indifference $\theta=1$ this is the weak statement $x^{*}=0$ for every
$0\le\theta<1$, i.e. the lenient auditor is the unique, $x$-independent,
best response for the whole interior of the type space and the
malpractice type is the one which strictly wants leniency.  The
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ is the only boundary case. ∎
public_text.3:
For the $x$--dependent part of the expected outlay write

$$
\ell(\theta ,x):=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x),
$$

so that up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}=k'(\theta)h'(x) .
$$

$1-\theta$ is strictly decreasing and $F$ is decreasing, hence

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
k(\theta)>0\;{\rm for}\;\theta<1,\;k(1)=0,
$$

and $k(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.  On the two point
support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
          =p(1)k(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  In
particular

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-perfect type and the
two auditors are indifferent for the perfectly truthful type.  Hence
with the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le \theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the disadvantage of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\bigl[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,\qquad 
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In the Spence–Mirrlees sense

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\Big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\Big]\,
   \Big[p(x)+xp'(x)\Big]<0
$$

whenever $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, so that $\partial C/\partial x$ is
decreasing in $\theta$.  The cost of moving $0\to1$ falls with
$\theta$ and the optimal strictness is weakly non-decreasing in
$\theta$.  In the binary $0/1$ formulation the best reply is the
constant $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$ and is
indifferent only at the knife edge $\theta=1$.  In the strict preference
sense there is therefore no interior $\theta$ at which a rise in
truthfulness strictly induces a strict move to a more lenient auditor;
the strictly monotone decreasing comparative static is vacuous, the
only boundary being the indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  Up to the
conventional tie break this is the trivial weak statement
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for every non-perfect type $\theta\in[0,1)$, with
$x^{*}=0$ the unique best reply for all $\theta<1$ and indifference at
$\theta=1$.  This is the reversal of the usual signalling intuition:
the more truthful type can afford the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ and the
reputation benefit $p(x)\downarrow$, so optimal $x^{*}$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$, not decreasing. ∎

1.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the relevant $x$ dependent part of expected payment
is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid
{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta) ,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+\ell (\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+k(\theta )h(x),
\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ can be dropped for the choice of $x$. On the
$0/1$ support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,
$$

so that with $t$ $x$-free

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ is decreasing and $F$ is decreasing, hence on $[0,1]$

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
$$

so that $k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, $k$ is strictly decreasing and

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad 
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 .
$$

Hence on the binary support

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non perfect type and the
perfectly truthful type is indifferent. With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

so that $x^{*}(\cdot)$ is constant on the interior of the type space.
The cost disadvantage of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$, $\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$
for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$, and, for $h(x)=xp(x)$ increasing,

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and $C$ has
decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  In the Spence-Mirrlees sense
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$; a higher $\theta$
makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In strict preference terms there is therefore no interior
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$.
The strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
$\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is vacuous on the interior,
the strictly decreasing set being empty. Modulo the conventional tie
break the weak dominance is

$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$, with the knife edge indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at $\theta=1$,

i.e. the lenient auditor is the unique best reply for every
non-perfect type $\theta<1$ and the usual statement is that the lenient
auditor is weakly optimal on the whole interior $[0,1)$, the only
non-trivial boundary being the indifference at the perfectly truthful
limit $\theta=1$. This is the familiar reversal of the signalling
intuition: the more truthful type can afford the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ and optimal strictness is weakly increasing in
truthfulness. ∎

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x)$
with $k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ and $h(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.
$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give $k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$,
$k(1)=0$, $k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and $k$ strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.

On the stated binary support $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so up to $t(\theta)$

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)k(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$.

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$ and
$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.
In differentiable form $\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)]<0$.

Hence $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.
With the usual tie break
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$,
i.e. the lenient auditor strictly dominates the strict one for every non-perfect
type and the perfectly truthful type is indifferent. The best reply is
constant $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$.

$\partial C/\partial x=(1-\theta)F(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ and
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=[p(x)+xp'(x)]k'(\theta)$
with $k'(\theta)<0$. Hence $\operatorname{sgn}\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=
-\operatorname{sgn}[p(x)+xp'(x)]=-\operatorname{sgn}h'(x)$.
For the binary support $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$ so $h$ is increasing and
$\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$; the cost disadvantage of
$x=1$ relative to $x=0$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$. In the Spence-Mirrlees
sense $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$; a higher $\theta$
makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In strict preference terms there is no interior $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$: the strictly monotone decrease
$x^{*}\downarrow\theta$ is vacuous, the strictly decreasing set is empty.
Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique best response on the whole interior
$\theta\in[0,1)$, with the knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at $\theta=1$.
This is the conventional reversal of the signalling intuition.

All colleagues in round 2 converge on this: $C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$
for $\theta<1$, strictly decreasing in $\theta$, $x^{*}=0$ for all non-perfect
types, indifference only at $\theta=1$. Disagreement is only wording strict vs
weak and tie-breaking at the top. The continuous-case nuance $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$
remains noted: with $p\downarrow$ fast enough $h$ can be decreasing and the sign
flips, but on the stated $0/1$ support $h(1)>h(0)$ so the binary result is unchanged.
With the discrete support $\{0,1\}$ the only strict preference for leniency is
$\theta=0$ and $\theta=1$ is indifferent.
reflection_text.3:

C(θ,x)=t(θ)+x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=t(θ)+k(θ)h(x), 
k(θ)=(1-θ)F(θ)>0, h(x)=xp(x)≥0,

and on the binary support

C(θ,0)=t(θ),  C(θ,1)=t(θ)+(1-θ)p(1)F(θ),

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=p(1)k(θ)=p(1)(1-θ)F(θ)≥0.

F↓ and 1-θ↓ ⇒ k'(θ)=-F(θ)+(1-θ)F'(θ)<0, k(1)=0, k(θ)>0 for θ<1.
Hence Δ(θ)>0 ⇔ θ<1, Δ(1)=0 and Δ'(θ)=p(1)[-F+(1-θ)F']<0,
Δ(θ2)<Δ(θ1) for θ2>θ1.  The extra expected penalty of the strict auditor
is strictly positive for every non-perfect type and strictly decreasing in
truthfulness.

Therefore with tie-break

x*(θ)=0 for 0≤θ<1,  x*(1)∈{0,1},  C(θ,0)<C(θ,1) for θ<1, C(1,0)=C(1,1).
The best reply is constant x*≡0 on the interior of the type space.  The
$x$-dependent part has decreasing differences in the usual Spence-Mirrlees
form

∂²C/∂θ∂x = [p(x)+xp'(x)][-F(θ)+(1-θ)F'(θ)] ,

so ∂C/∂x is decreasing in θ whenever h'(x)=p+xp'>0.  With the stated
decreasing p(x) the sign of h' is ambiguous; the binary result is
independent of it: a higher θ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper,
x* is weakly non-decreasing in θ in the set order.  In particular the
strict cost disadvantage of x=1 relative to x=0 falls with θ and
vanishes only at θ=1.

Hence in strict preference terms there is no interior pair θ2>θ1 with
x*(θ2)<x*(θ1).  The strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
θ↑⇒x*↓ is vacuous, the strictly decreasing set is empty.  Weakly the
lenient auditor is the unique strict best reply for every non-perfect type,
x*=0 on [0,1), essentially 0<θ<1, with the knife-edge indifference
Δ(1)=0 at the perfectly truthful limit.  On the two-point support this is
x*(0)=0 strictly and x*(1) indifferent.  The disagreement in the round is
purely terminological between the empty strict set and the weak statement
x*≡0 on the interior 0≤θ<1, i.e. 0<θ<1, the familiar reversal of the

x(1-θ) and optimal strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness. ∎

1.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the $x$ dependent part of expected payment is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ can be dropped for the choice of $x$.  On the stated
$0/1$ support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,
$$

so that up to $t$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
          =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give on $[0,1]$

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,\;
k(\theta)>0\;\; \theta<1,
$$

hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,\qquad 
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

and

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).
$$

With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type space.  The extra
expected penalty of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly positive for every non-perfect type and is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness.  With $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =h'(x)k'(\theta)<0,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and $C$ has
decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$.  The cost disadvantage of
$x=1$ relative to $x=0$ falls with $\theta$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict
auditor relatively cheaper.

In strict preference terms the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$.  There is
therefore no interior pair $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the strictly monotone decreasing
comparative static $\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is
vacuous on the interior and the strictly decreasing set is empty.  In
the weak ordering the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict best
response for every non-perfect type,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, with the knife edge
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  This is
the conventional statement $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$, essentially
$0<\theta<1$, and optimal strictness is weakly increasing in
truthfulness.  Up to the conventional tie break the strictly more
lenient move never occurs. ∎

2.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$

$$
\ell(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{ {\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid{\rm refusal}\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),
$$
$$
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)\ge0,
$$
$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x).
$$

On the binary support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that with $t$ dropped

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give on $[0,1]$

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
\qquad k(\theta)>0\;{\rm for}\;\theta<1,
$$

hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).
$$

With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly positive on the
interior and strictly decreasing in $\theta$.
In differentiable notation, with $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$,

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(x)k'(\theta)
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$, $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing
in $\theta$; a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively
cheaper.

Hence on the $0/1$ support the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type space.  In strict preference
terms there is no interior pair $\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$.  The strictly monotone decreasing
comparative static $\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is
vacuous, the strictly decreasing set is empty.  Up to the conventional
tie break the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict best response
for every non-perfect type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$,
essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the knife-edge indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, at the perfectly truthful limit.
This is the familiar reversal of the signalling intuition: optimal
strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness and the lenient auditor
dominates on $[0,1)$. ∎

6.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta )$ the $x$-dependent part of the
expected outlay is

$$
\ell (\theta ,x) ={\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta )
        =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta )h(x) ,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+k(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 .
$$

On the stated binary support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that with $t(\theta )$ $x$-free

$$
\Delta (\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
$$

$k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and $k$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.
Hence on the $0/1$ support

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

$$
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

i.e. 

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1),\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1) .
$$

With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad
0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

the lenient auditor strictly dominates the strict one for every
non-perfect type and the perfectly truthful type is indifferent.
The cost disadvantage of the strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly positive on the
interior and strictly decreasing in truthfulness,

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so that

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0
$$

when $h'(x)>0$ and $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.
In the Spence–Mirrlees sense $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in
$\theta$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$; a
higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In strict preference terms $x^{*}(\cdot)$ is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, essentially
$0<\theta<1$.  There is therefore no interior pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$.
The strictly monotone comparative static
$\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is vacuous on the interior
and the strictly decreasing set is empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor
$x=0$ is the unique best reply for every non-perfect type, $C(\theta,0)
\le C(\theta,1)$ with strict inequality for $0\le\theta<1$, with the
knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful limit
$\theta=1$.  This is the usual statement $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$,
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the familiar reversal of the signalling
intuition. ∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$

$$
\ell (\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid no\;report\}F(\theta)
            =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x) .
$$

On the $0/1$ support $t(\theta)$ is $x$-free and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$F\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$ give

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
\qquad k(\theta)>0\;\;{\rm for}\;\;\theta<1,
$$

hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 .
$$

In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\quad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

so with the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type space.  The extra
expected penalty of the strict auditor $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)
F(\theta)$ is strictly positive on the interior and strictly decreasing
in $\theta$,

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1}),\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

and with $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =k'(\theta)h'(x)<0,
$$

$C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and
$\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$.  Hence the cost
disadvantage of $x=1$ relative to $x=0$ falls with truthfulness and
optimal strictness is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$.

In strict preference terms the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  There is therefore no interior pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$:
the strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
$\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is vacuous and the strictly
decreasing set is empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict best response for every non-perfect type, $C(\theta,0)<
C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the
knife-edge indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit
$\theta=1$.  This is the familiar reversal of the signalling intuition:
the lenient auditor dominates on the whole economically relevant
interior and a rise in truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively
cheaper but never strictly optimal on $(0,1)$. ∎

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The $x$-free tax can be dropped for the choice of auditor. With
${\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}=x(1-\theta)$ and ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS}\mid{\rm refusal}\}=p(x)$

$$
\ell(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge0,
$$

$$
C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x).
$$

On the admissible binary support

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)k(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give $k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$,
$k(1)=0$ and $k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,\qquad 
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})\;\;\hbox{for }\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $\Delta$ is strictly positive on the interior and strictly decreasing in
truthfulness.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\quad0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

so with the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent.  The extra expected penalty of the strict
auditor $\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is therefore the saving from
staying with the lenient technology, it is $>0$ for every non-perfect type and
it is monotone decreasing in $\theta$.  With $h'(x)>0$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}=k'(\theta)h'(x)<0,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta,x)$.

Hence for any $\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$ both types remain at the unique
strict best reply $x^{*}=0$.  The lenient auditor is the unique best reply on
the whole interior of the type space and the advantage of leniency over
strictness,
$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)>0$, shrinks with $\theta$ but stays
positive until the knife edge $\theta=1$.  In the economically relevant weak
best-response sense the firm continues to choose the lenient auditor $x=0$ as
truthfulness rises, i.e. higher $\theta$ is associated with the lenient choice
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior.

On the binary support this is normally reported as weak optimality of
leniency on $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the conventional
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the perfectly truthful limit.  The monotone
decreasing of the leniency premium
$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ is the
comparative static that is quoted as “more truthful $\Rightarrow$ (weakly)
more lenient’’ on the interior, the relevant set being the interior
$\theta<1$, up to the degenerate boundary $\theta=1$. ∎

$$

x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$
$x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$, i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type
space.  The extra expected penalty of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly positive on the interior and strictly decreasing in
truthfulness, $\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0
$$

for $h'(x)>0$, $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$ and
$C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  Hence the cost
disadvantage of $x=1$ relative to $x=0$ falls with $\theta$ and optimal
strictness is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$,
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.

In strict preference terms the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  There is therefore no interior pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the
strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
$\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is vacuous and the strictly
decreasing set is empty.  Modulo the conventional tie break the lenient
auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict best response for every non-perfect
type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, i.e. essentially for
$0<\theta<1$, with the knife-edge indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$,
$\Delta(1)=0$, at the perfectly truthful limit.  This is the familiar
reversal of the signalling intuition: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict
auditor relatively cheaper and the lenient technology is strictly
dominant on the whole economically relevant interior $0\le\theta<1$. ∎

5.text:
With the $x$--free tax $t(\theta)$ dropped put
$$
\ell(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$
$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x) .
$$
On the two point support
$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$
so that up to $t(\theta)$
$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$
$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give
$k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, $k(1)=0$ and
$k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  Hence
$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$
and
$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1).
$$
With the usual tie break
$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$
and with $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$
$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(x)k'(\theta)<0,
$$
so that $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$, $C$ has
decreasing differences and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in
$\theta$.  The extra expected penalty of the strict auditor,
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$, is strictly positive on the
interior and strictly decreasing in $\theta$,
$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})\quad\hbox{for }\theta_{2}>
\theta_{1},
$$
so a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.
In particular
$$
C(\theta_{2},1)-C(\theta_{2},0)-\big[C(\theta_{1},1)-C(\theta_{1},0)\big]
 =[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})]h(1)<0,\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$
and on the binary support the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$.  Up to the
knife edge $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict best response for every non-perfect type.

Hence in strict preference terms there is no interior pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$.
The strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
$\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is vacuous on the interior;
the strictly decreasing set is empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor is
the unique optimal choice on the economically relevant interior,
$x^{*}=0$ for every $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the
conventional indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the perfectly truthful limit
$\theta=1$.  This is the familiar reversal of the signalling intuition:
optimal strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness and the lenient
technology dominates for all non-perfect types. ∎

8.text:

 =[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})][h(x_{2})-h(x_{1})]<0

In strict preference terms there is therefore no interior pair

$$

differences in $(\theta,x)$.

strictness,

positive until the knife edge $\theta=1$.  In the economically relevant weak
best-response sense the firm continues to choose the lenient auditor $x=0$ as
truthfulness rises, i.e. higher $\theta$ is associated with the lenient choice

leniency on $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the conventional

decreasing of the leniency premium
$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ is the
comparative static that is quoted as “more truthful $\Rightarrow$ (weakly)

$$

C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) .

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
\qquad k(\theta)>0\;{\rm for}\;\theta<1,
$$

so that

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 .

$$

$$

0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},

expected penalty of the strict auditor

$$

truthfulness, $\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for

$$

   =h'(x)k'(\theta)<0,

differences and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing in $\theta$;
a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the knife edge $\theta=1$.  In strict
preference terms there is no interior pair $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$
with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the strictly monotone
decreasing comparative static $\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$
is vacuous on the interior and the strictly decreasing set is empty.

every non-perfect type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$,

\ell(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta)
        =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x) ,
\qquad 
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$$
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,\qquad 
h(0)=0,\;h(1)=p(1) .
$$

On the $0\!-\!1$ support $t(\theta)$ can be dropped for the choice of
$x$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad
 C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

so that with $t$ dropped

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,
\qquad k(\theta)>0\;{\rm for}\;\theta<1,
$$

hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad0\le \theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).
$$

With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0 ,\qquad 
0\le\theta<1 ,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$.  The extra expected penalty of the strict
auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is $>0$ on the interior and strictly decreasing in truthfulness,
$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.
With $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(x)k'(\theta)<0 ,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$, $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and optimal strictness is weakly
non-decreasing in $\theta$.  In particular

$$
C(\theta_{2},1)-C(\theta_{2},0)-\big[C(\theta_{1},1)-C(\theta_{1},0)\big]
 =\big[k(\theta_{2})-k(\theta_{1})\big]p(1)<0,
\qquad \theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the cost disadvantage of $x=1$ relative to $x=0$ falls with $\theta$.

Hence on the $0/1$ support the best reply is the constant map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type space.  In strict preference
terms there is no pair $\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$: the strictly monotone decreasing
comparative static $\theta\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\downarrow$ is
vacuous on $0<\theta<1$ and the strictly decreasing set is empty.
Modulo the conventional tie break the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the
unique strict best response for every non-perfect type,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$,
with the knife edge indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, $\Delta(1)=0$, at the
perfectly truthful limit.  This is the familiar reversal of the
signalling intuition: optimal strictness is weakly increasing in
truthfulness and the lenient technology strictly dominates on the whole
economically relevant interior; the saving from leniency,
$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)$, is strictly positive for
$\theta<1$ and monotone decreasing to $0$ as $\theta\to1$. ∎

$$

       =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=k(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$h(x)=xp(x)\ge0$, and $t(\theta)$ can be dropped for the choice of $x$.
On the admissible binary support $h(0)=0,\;h(1)=p(1)>0$,

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,
$$

so that with $t$ dropped

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)k(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$F\downarrow$ gives $k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$,
$k(1)=0$ and $k(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, hence $k$ is strictly
decreasing on $[0,1]$ and

$$

\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0 ,
$$

i.e.

$$

$$

$$

0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

so that on the economically relevant interior $x^{*}\equiv0$.  The
extra expected penalty of the strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ for every non-perfect type
is strictly decreasing in truthfulness,

Up to the $x$–free tax the relevant cost is

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta)
      =t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+k(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$
k(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 ,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ can be dropped for the choice of $x$.  
On the $0/1$ support

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta), \qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

so that up to $t$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)
      =p(1)k(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0 .
$$

$F\!\downarrow$ and $1-\theta\!\downarrow$ give

$$
k'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad k(1)=0,\qquad
k(\theta)>0\;\;{\rm for}\;\;\theta<1,
$$

hence

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,\qquad
\Delta'(\theta)=p(1)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1) \quad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).
$$

With the usual tie break

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior of the type space.  In particular

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(x)k'(\theta)=\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
$$

so $\partial C/\partial x$ is decreasing in $\theta$, $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly non-decreasing
in $\theta$.  The extra expected penalty of the strict auditor

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is $>0$ for every non–perfect type and is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness, the advantage of leniency
$C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)$ shrinking with $\theta$ and
vanishing only at the knife edge $\theta=1$.

Hence on the binary support the best reply is the constant lenient map
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  In strict preference terms there is no pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$;
the strictly monotone decreasing comparative static
$\theta\!\uparrow\Rightarrow x^{*}\!\downarrow$ is vacuous and the strictly
decreasing set is empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict best response for every non-perfect type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$
for $0\le\theta<1$, essentially $0<\theta<1$, with the conventional
indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, $\Delta(1)=0$, at the perfectly truthful
limit.  Optimal strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness; a rise
in $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper but never
strictly optimal on the economically relevant interior.  This is the
usual statement $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$. ∎
